extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of communication studies, media history, and history of technology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for researching and judging historical and theoretical work in communication/media studies (exemplified by Harold Innis and the Chicago School). Emphasizes method, historical/contextual grounding, and the political/geographic-material dimensions of communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolt against formalism / interdisciplinary approach
rubrics_metrics.description: “They attempted to return social studies to a branch of history and to emphasize the interdisciplinary nature of social knowledge.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor research that crosses disciplinary boundaries (history, geography, economics, political science) rather than narrow formalism. Example: Chicago School’s attempt to integrate social studies with historical methods; ransack experience without regard to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication as cultural formation (not merely information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication is “the entire process whereby a culture is brought into existence, maintained in time, and sedimented into institutions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat communication as bound up with art, architecture, custom, ritual, and politics — study how media produce and maintain cultural institutions rather than only transmitting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the nature and conditions of public life / public sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should try to “work through the conditions under which the public sphere gives rise to rational and critical discourse and action.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how media and communications create or erode publics (e.g., concerns about the ‘vanishing public’), and assess effects on rational discourse, enlightened public opinion, and democratic deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject naive romanticism / critique technological sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarship should be “purged of the inherited romanticism of the Chicago School” and resist harmless romanticism about technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid celebratory assumptions that technology inevitably democratizes or liberates; interrogate claims of progressive liberation and beware rhetoric of the technological sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historicism / contextual adaptation of scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: “All scholarship must be and inevitably is adapted to the time and place of its creation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate analysis in its material, cultural, and historical context; examine how the conditions of production shape theory. Use Marx’s injunction to analyze material conditions as prerequisite to critical transcendence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological mix: historical, empirical, interpretive, and critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Innis provided “a model of scholarly investigation that was historical, empirical, interpretive, and critical.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine exhumation of archival/historical records (empirical) with interpretive work on meanings and a critical stance informed by humane/civilized values. Avoid purely formal or value-free models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verification-model universals; attend to particularities
rubrics_metrics.description: The central terms Innis used “were not the terms of a verification model” — variations in history and geography demanded concomitant variation in social theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not privilege universal, law-like explanations; derive theory from concrete historical/geographical variation. Use flexible, locally-grounded concepts rather than ironclad laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support pluralistic centers of scholarship / resist monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Committed to the notion of “pluralistic centers of scholarship as essential to cultural stability.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value decentralized intellectual life and multiple centers of production of knowledge; be alert to how centralization of media/institutions can threaten cultural stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze technological spatial and temporal biases (space-/time-binding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend to “the limitations of technology, the spatial and temporal bias inherent in technology” and the distinction between space-binding and time-binding cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how specific media favor spatial extension (empire, movement, expansion) or temporal continuity (tradition, ritual), and how that bias shapes social organization and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate monopolies of knowledge and media imperialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine “the monopolies of knowledge toward which [technologies] tend and which they support.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how infrastructures and media concentrate cultural power (e.g., New York hegemony, paper/pulp trade, back-tier/metropole relations) and how trade/technology produce asymmetric influence between centers and peripheries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider dual functional models of communication: domination and therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: Postwar models cast communication either as “a mode of domination” or as “a form of therapy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize multiple normative/functional interpretations of media (control vs. anxiety-relief/therapy) and that theoretical models can become templates for practice; analyze both their descriptive and performative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground studies in material infrastructures, geography, and trade routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use polarities such as “metropole and hinterland, center and margin, capital and periphery” to explain communication and cultural relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine concrete transport/communication infrastructures (canals, railroads, telegraph, wire services) and their spatial organization to explain cultural flows and inequalities (e.g., Erie Canal, Illinois Central Railroad, telegraph effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical exhumation of historical record over abstract laws
rubrics_metrics.description: He “attempted to exhume the actual historical record and not those ironclad laws of development.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize archival and factual investigation (staples, beaver biology, paper trade) that can overturn abstract stage theories (e.g., frontier hypothesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze how technologies change interests, symbols, and community
rubrics_metrics.description: “Changes in communication technology affected culture by altering the structure of interests (the things thought about), by changing the character of symbols (the things thought with), and by changing the nature of community (the arena in which thought developed).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media effects, specify effects on cognitive focus (what societies think about), symbolic repertoires (languages/concepts), and social units of organization (local vs. national communities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pierce organic metaphors that mask power relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique “organic metaphors that so often led the Chicago scholars astray and masked the facts of history, geography, and power.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of holistic/organismic analogies that obscure centralized control; instead locate controlling elements, centralized brains, and how knowledge/communication are monopolized by particular groups.
